subject: Ch1: Introduction & Language-Processing Tools (Hard)
description: Hard-level MCQs on the structure of a compiler, phases vs passes, analysis/synthesis, and the language-processing system: preprocessor, assembler, linker, loader, interpreters, JIT, cross-compilers, and bootstrapping.

questions.text: A compiler for language S is written in language I and produces target code for machine T. For it to RUN, the host machine must already be able to execute:
options: Any of S, I, or T equally, as all three languages must be natively supported by the host
I, the implementation language in which the compiler itself is written, because a program can only run where its own implementation language is supported
T, since the machine has to be capable of running the target code that is ultimately emitted
S, because the host must understand every construct of the source language being accepted
questions.shortExplanation: A program runs on the machine that can execute its implementation language.
questions.explanation: In T-diagram terms the implementation language I determines where the compiler can run; S is what it accepts and T is what it emits, but execution requires support for I.

questions.text: Which statement about phases versus passes is correct?
options: The number of passes in any compiler is fixed and must always equal the exact number of phases
Several phases can be grouped into one pass, and one phase may also be split across passes
A pass is always strictly smaller than a single phase and can never contain a complete phase within it
Passes are purely logical sub-tasks while phases are the physical traversals that read and write the program
questions.shortExplanation: Phases are logical; passes are physical groupings and need not match one-to-one.
questions.explanation: Phases are logical sub-tasks; a pass reads input once and writes output once. Multiple phases may share a pass, and the mapping is not one-to-one.

questions.text: Forward references to labels defined later force a one-pass assembler to fail, which is precisely why a two-pass assembler:
options: Builds the symbol table of label addresses in pass one before emitting any code in pass two
Repeats the entire lexical analysis stage a second time purely as a redundant safety check
Performs all of its machine-code optimization work exclusively during the second and final pass over the source
Loads the assembled program directly into main memory while it is still executing its first pass
questions.shortExplanation: Pass one resolves all label addresses; pass two emits code.
questions.explanation: Because a forward reference is unknown when first seen, pass one records every label's address in the symbol table so pass two can emit correct addresses.

questions.text: Which task is performed by the linker but NOT by the loader?
options: Bringing the complete program image from secondary storage into main memory before execution begins
Setting the program counter to the entry point so the loaded process can start running immediately
Allocating the run-time stack space that the executing program will use for its activation records
Resolving references to a symbol that is defined in another, separately compiled object module by combining those modules together into a single program image
questions.shortExplanation: Cross-module symbol resolution is linking, not loading.
questions.explanation: The linker combines object modules and resolves external/cross-module references; the loader places the resulting image in memory and starts it.

questions.text: An interpreter and a compiler differ MOST fundamentally in that the interpreter:
options: Always executes the program strictly faster than the equivalent fully compiled native code would
Does not produce any separate, standalone target program that is itself able to run on its own
Cannot detect any kind of semantic error in the program at all, not even type mismatches
Never builds an intermediate representation of any kind while processing the source program
questions.shortExplanation: Interpreters execute the source; no standalone target is produced.
questions.explanation: The defining difference is the absence of a separate target program: the interpreter performs the actions of the source directly (it may still build an IR and check errors).

questions.text: Bootstrapping a compiler for language L using a 'quick and dirty' subset compiler illustrates that:
options: The loader for the target system must always be fully written and tested before the compiler exists
A compiler for a given language can never under any circumstances whatsoever be written in that very same source language itself
Cross-compilation between two machines is fundamentally impossible unless an interpreter is also present
The first version is built in another language or subset, then used to compile the full self-hosting compiler
questions.shortExplanation: Bootstrapping breaks the circularity with an initial compiler.
questions.explanation: An initial compiler (in another language or for a subset) compiles a fuller version written in L, which can then recompile itself — the bootstrapping process.

questions.text: To port a self-hosting compiler from machine A to a new machine B, the usual technique is to:
options: Run the existing machine-A executable directly on machine B without any modification whatsoever
Rewrite the entire compiler from scratch in the native assembly language of the new machine B
Install an interpreter on machine B whose job is to read and execute machine A's binary code
Retarget the back-end so that it emits machine code for B, and then cross-compile the compiler itself on the existing machine A to obtain a compiler that runs on B
questions.shortExplanation: Retarget the back-end, then cross-compile on the old host.
questions.explanation: You change the code generator to produce B's instructions and run that compiler on A (cross-compilation) to obtain a compiler that runs on B.

questions.text: Which error is the EARLIEST phase able to detect that the lexeme `12abc` is malformed as a number followed by identifier rules?
options: It depends on the token patterns; it may be scanned as `12` then `abc`, deferring any error to the parser
It can only ever be discovered later during the semantic-analysis phase when types are being checked
It is unconditionally and always a lexical error in absolutely every programming language, no matter what token patterns or scanning rules happen to apply
It is detected by the linker while it is resolving external references across the object modules
questions.shortExplanation: Maximal-munch may split it into valid tokens, so it can be a syntax issue.
questions.explanation: With typical patterns the scanner emits num(12) then id(abc) by longest-match; whether that is an error is then a syntactic question, not necessarily lexical.

questions.text: The PRIMARY engineering reason to introduce a machine-independent intermediate representation is to:
options: Eliminate the semantic-analysis phase entirely from the front-end of the compiler pipeline
Make the symbol table completely unnecessary so that identifier attributes need not be stored anywhere
Reduce the number of front-ends and back-ends needed for m languages and n machines from m×n to m+n
Guarantee that the compiled program will contain absolutely no runtime errors of any kind
questions.shortExplanation: A shared IR turns m×n compilers into m front-ends + n back-ends.
questions.explanation: With a common IR, each of m languages needs one front-end and each of n machines one back-end, giving m+n components instead of m×n.

questions.text: Static linking versus dynamic linking: a key DISADVANTAGE of static linking is that:
options: It is fundamentally incapable of resolving any external references between separately compiled modules
It always requires a virtual machine to be present in order to execute the resulting program
Library code is duplicated in every executable and updates require relinking
It can only ever be carried out at run time, never at the earlier link stage of the build
questions.shortExplanation: Static linking copies libraries in, causing duplication and relink-on-update.
questions.explanation: Statically linked libraries are baked into each executable, wasting space and forcing a relink when the library changes; dynamic linking shares one copy at load/run time.

questions.text: Which of the following is FALSE about the symbol table?
options: It can be initially created during lexical analysis and then progressively refined during semantic analysis
It stores important attributes such as the type, scope, and storage information of program identifiers
It is consulted by both the analysis and the synthesis phases throughout the entire compilation process
It is discarded immediately after parsing completes, so none of the later phases such as semantic analysis or code generation are able to consult it at all
questions.shortExplanation: The symbol table persists well beyond parsing.
questions.explanation: Statement D is false: the symbol table is needed for semantic analysis and later phases, so it is not discarded right after parsing.

questions.text: A JIT compiler blurs the compiler/interpreter line because it:
options: Runs exclusively on a machine that is different from the one on which the compiled code will execute
Translates the program's entire source text into machine code well before any execution can begin
Compiles selected hot code (often bytecode) into native machine code during execution, then runs it
Only ever interprets the program statement by statement and never generates any machine code at all
questions.shortExplanation: JIT compiles at run time, then executes native code.
questions.explanation: A JIT translates hot code to machine code while the program runs, combining interpreter startup with compiled-speed execution of frequently used paths.

questions.text: Macro expansion by a preprocessor differs from a function call because macro expansion:
options: Allocates a fresh activation record on the run-time stack each time the macro name is encountered
Is carried out entirely by the linker while it combines the object modules of the program
Requires full type checking of every argument exactly as an ordinary function call would demand
Is a purely textual substitution carried out by the preprocessor before compilation begins, incurring no run-time call, stack frame, or call overhead at all
questions.shortExplanation: Macros are textual, pre-compilation, no call overhead or type checks.
questions.explanation: Preprocessor macros substitute text before compilation; unlike function calls they incur no stack frame and are not type-checked as calls.

questions.text: Relocatable machine code produced by an assembler differs from absolute code in that relocatable code:
options: Uses relative addresses that can later be adjusted by the linker or loader when modules combine
Must always be executed indirectly by an interpreter rather than running on the hardware directly
Can never be linked together with any other separately assembled object modules under any condition
Is in fact identical to the original source code that the programmer originally wrote by hand
questions.shortExplanation: Relocatable addresses are adjustable at link/load time.
questions.explanation: Relocatable code leaves addresses unresolved/relative so the linker or relocating loader can fix them up; absolute code has fixed addresses.

questions.text: Which ordering correctly reflects increasing abstraction from hardware?
options: Machine language closest to the bare hardware, then assembly language as a symbolic layer above it, and finally the high-level language as the most abstract
High-level language, then machine language, and finally assembly as the most abstract symbolic layer
High-level language, then assembly language, and finally machine language closest to the bare hardware
Assembly language first, then machine language, and lastly the most abstract high-level language
questions.shortExplanation: Machine < assembly < high-level in abstraction.
questions.explanation: Machine language is closest to hardware, assembly is a symbolic layer above it, and high-level languages are the most abstract.

questions.text: Separate compilation of modules is enabled chiefly by the:
options: Interpreter, which executes each individual module on its own immediately after that module is written
Linker, which resolves inter-module references after each module has been compiled fully independently
Scanner, which lets all modules share one single global character buffer during lexical analysis
Loader, which interprets the portable bytecode of each module as the program is brought into memory
questions.shortExplanation: The linker stitches independently compiled modules together.
questions.explanation: Each module is compiled to an object file with unresolved external symbols; the linker later resolves them, enabling separate compilation.

questions.text: A cross-compiler is essential when:
options: Only straightforward interpretation of the source program is required rather than full compilation
The program being compiled contains no external references to any separately compiled module at all
The target machine cannot host the compiler itself, e.g. an embedded device
The source language and the target language happen to be exactly identical to one another
questions.shortExplanation: Cross-compilers target machines that can't run the compiler.
questions.explanation: For small/embedded targets that cannot host a full toolchain, a cross-compiler runs on a capable host and emits code for the target.

questions.text: Which is the BEST description of the boundary between front-end and back-end?
options: The front-end performs target register allocation and the rest of the machine-dependent code generation
Front-end produces a semantically checked intermediate representation; back-end maps it to the target
The back-end is responsible for parsing the source and carrying out all of the semantic analysis
The front-end finishes immediately after lexical analysis and produces nothing more than a token stream
questions.shortExplanation: Front-end → checked IR; back-end → target code.
questions.explanation: The front-end (lex, syntax, semantic) yields a verified IR; the back-end (optimization, code generation) is machine-dependent.

questions.text: An absolute loader, compared with a relocating loader, requires that:
options: The linking step be skipped entirely so that all module combination happens during loading instead
The program be loaded at a fixed, predetermined address that was already assumed back at assembly time, since the loader performs no relocation
The machine code of the program be interpreted one line at a time as it is brought into memory
Every symbol in the program be deliberately left unresolved right up until the moment of loading
questions.shortExplanation: Absolute loaders need a fixed load address.
questions.explanation: An absolute loader places code at the exact addresses assumed at assembly time; a relocating loader can adjust addresses at load time.

questions.text: Why can a single-pass compiler struggle with languages allowing use-before-declaration?
options: It is fundamentally unable to read the source file from beginning to end even a single time
It will inevitably run out of available memory whenever the input program grows beyond a few lines
Information needed to resolve a forward-referenced name is not yet available in one traversal
It completely lacks any lexical analyzer and therefore cannot turn the source into tokens at all
questions.shortExplanation: One pass lacks later-declared info for forward references.
questions.explanation: A single traversal may reach a use before the declaration is seen, so the needed attributes are unavailable, motivating multiple passes or backpatching.

questions.text: Which statement about analysis vs synthesis is TRUE?
options: Analysis breaks the program into pieces and imposes a grammatical structure; synthesis constructs the target
Analysis is the part of the compiler that is responsible for performing the final code generation step
Synthesis is the part of the compiler that carries out the lexical analysis of the incoming source text
Synthesis is an entirely machine-independent activity that never needs to know anything at all about the target architecture or its instruction set
questions.shortExplanation: Analysis decomposes/checks; synthesis builds the target.
questions.explanation: The analysis (front-end) part decomposes and validates the source into an IR; the synthesis (back-end) part generates the target program from it.

questions.text: A 'hybrid' compiler such as the typical Java toolchain is characterized by:
options: Compiling the source to platform-neutral bytecode that a VM later interprets or just-in-time builds
Skipping the compilation stage altogether and simply interpreting the raw source text line by line
Producing only assembly language as its output, which then needs no further processing by any tool
Compiling the source directly down to the native code of one single platform and nothing else at all
questions.shortExplanation: Compile to bytecode; VM interprets/JITs it.
questions.explanation: Java source compiles to portable bytecode executed by the JVM, which interprets and/or JIT-compiles it — a hybrid of compilation and interpretation.

questions.text: Which pair lists tools that BOTH consult or build a symbol table of names/addresses?
options: The source-code editor together with the debugger, both indexing identifier names and locations
The loader together with the preprocessor, both maintaining a table of names and their addresses
The interpreter together with the absolute loader, each building its own table of label addresses
Compiler and assembler
questions.shortExplanation: Both compiler and assembler use symbol tables.
questions.explanation: The compiler maintains a symbol table of identifiers; the assembler maintains a table of labels/addresses — both rely on symbol tables.

questions.text: Type checking of an expression like `x + y` where one is a string is BEST classified as:
options: A static-semantic error detected at compile time, because the rules governing operand types are part of the language's static semantics rather than its grammar
A dynamic error that can only ever be caught while the program is actually running on the machine
A syntactic error that arises directly from a violation of the grammar rules of the language
A lexical error that the scanner reports while it is still grouping characters into individual tokens
questions.shortExplanation: Type incompatibility is a static-semantic (compile-time) error.
questions.explanation: Static semantics include type rules checked at compile time; an incompatible `+` operand is a static-semantic error, not lexical or purely syntactic.

questions.text: The output that the COMPILER (proper) typically hands to the assembler is:
options: A completely linked executable file that is ready to be loaded into memory and run
Assembly (or symbolic target) code
A fully loaded, running process that has already begun executing on the target machine
A stream of tokens such as the one the lexical analyzer hands forward to the parser
questions.shortExplanation: Compiler → assembly; assembler → object code.
questions.explanation: In the classic pipeline the compiler emits assembly language, which the assembler then turns into relocatable object code.

questions.text: Which is NOT a valid reason to split compilation into multiple passes?
options: To handle forward references cleanly so that names used before their declaration can still be resolved
To enable powerful optimizations that need a complete global view of the entire program at once
To cleanly separate the machine-independent work from the machine-dependent work of the compiler
To reduce memory by never holding an IR
questions.shortExplanation: Multi-pass generally needs an IR between passes, not less of one.
questions.explanation: Multiple passes typically require storing an intermediate form between them; reducing memory by avoiding any IR is not a reason for multi-pass design.

questions.text: In the language-processing system, the component that may run BEFORE the compiler is the:
options: The loader, which brings the finished executable program image into main memory to run it
The linker, which combines the separately compiled object modules into one program image
Preprocessor
The assembler, which translates symbolic assembly code into relocatable machine object code
questions.shortExplanation: Preprocessor precedes the compiler.
questions.explanation: The preprocessor transforms the source (macros, includes) and feeds the result to the compiler; linker, assembler, and loader come after.

questions.text: Which best explains why interpreters give better error diagnostics during development?
options: They first compile the whole program down to heavily optimized native machine code before running it
They execute the source statement by statement, so errors are reported in source terms as they occur
They skip the semantic-analysis stage entirely and therefore have fewer phases that can ever fail
They are constructed in such a way that they simply never encounter any runtime errors at all
questions.shortExplanation: Source-level, stepwise execution yields precise diagnostics.
questions.explanation: Because the interpreter works directly on source constructs as they run, it can map errors back to source lines immediately, aiding debugging.

questions.text: A program that translates C++ into C so an existing C compiler can be reused is a:
options: Source-to-source compiler, also called a transpiler, mapping one high-level language to another
A dynamic linker that resolves references to shared library code at load time or during execution
A bytecode interpreter that directly executes platform-neutral instructions
A cross-assembler that turns symbolic assembly for one machine into the object code of another machine
questions.shortExplanation: High-level to high-level translation is transpilation.
questions.explanation: Translating one high-level language to another (C++ → C) is source-to-source compilation, after which a standard C compiler finishes the job.

questions.text: Which statement about the grouping of phases is MOST accurate?
options: Lexical analysis, syntax analysis, and semantic analysis must each be implemented as its own separate pass
Each phase is required to write all of its output to disk before the following phase is allowed to begin
The front-end phases are often combined into one pass driven by the parser calling the scanner
Code generation must always be carried out before semantic analysis is performed on the program
questions.shortExplanation: Front-end phases commonly share one parser-driven pass.
questions.explanation: In practice the parser drives the scanner on demand and invokes semantic actions, so the front-end phases are frequently fused into a single pass.
